questions.q: Which substance does NOT give a violet colour in the biuret test?
questions.explain: A violet colour needs two or more peptide (–CO–NH–) bonds. A dipeptide has only one, so the solution stays blue, while a tripeptide, proteins and biuret itself are positive.

questions.q: Biuret is prepared by heating urea to about 150 °C. The correctly balanced equation is:
questions.explain: Two urea molecules condense and one ammonia molecule is given off. Writing the equation without NH₃ is the common mistake; the reverse isomerisation to ammonium cyanate is unrelated.

questions.q: The violet colour in the biuret test is due to:
options: Oxidation of side chains by Cu²⁺
Reaction of biuret present in the reagent
Coordination of peptide nitrogen atoms to Cu²⁺ in alkaline solution
questions.explain: In strong alkali the peptide N–H protons are displaced and several neighbouring nitrogens of one chain chelate Cu²⁺, giving a violet complex. The reagent contains no biuret, and Cu₂O is the result of reducing-sugar tests, not this one.

questions.q: Sodium potassium tartrate is added to ready-made biuret reagent in order to:
options: Chelate Cu²⁺ and keep it in solution in the strongly alkaline medium
Hydrolyse the protein into amino acids
questions.explain: Tartrate holds Cu²⁺ as a complex so that it stays dissolved when NaOH or KOH is present. The test itself needs an alkaline medium, and copper stays in the +2 state.
